The right patient, every time

Before any test, medicine or procedure, confirm two identifiers:

  • Full name
  • Date of birth or medical record number

Ask the patient to say them, then match the wristband or record. Never use a room or bed number.

Dr. Omar: Two identifiers, every time: the full name and the date of birth or record number. Ask the patient to say them, then check the band. A room number is not an identifier: patients move.

Identifier or not?

Flip each card. Is it a safe patient identifier?

Noor: Flip the cards. Three are safe identifiers, one is a trap I've seen catch good nurses.

Two patients, one name

Noor · Safety liaison

Two patients named Mohammed Al-Harbi are waiting for blood tests. You call the name and one of them stands up. (Fictional training example.)

Score: 0

He walks over and holds out his arm. What do you do?

  • Best choice. Two identifiers, said by the patient and matched to the band, catch exactly this mix-up.

  • Risky. Two patients share that name: answering to it proves nothing. Ask for a second identifier.

  • A seat or room number is a location, not an identifier. Use the name plus date of birth or record number.

His date of birth does not match the request. What next?

  • Right. A mismatch means stop. You just prevented a wrong-patient result.

  • Never. A mislabelled sample can lead to the wrong treatment for both patients.

  • A colleague's memory is not an identifier. Check the identifiers against the request.

Noor: I once nearly drew blood from the wrong Mr Al-Harbi. The wristband stopped me. Your turn.

Find the fire safety equipment

Open every item. Know where these are before you need them.

0/8

Select a region to see its details.

Smoke detector

Senses smoke early and triggers the alarm. Never cover or tamper with it.

Heat detector

Triggers the alarm when the temperature rises fast — used where smoke detectors would false-alarm.

Sprinkler

Releases water automatically over a fire. Keep the space below it clear; never hang anything from it.

Call point

Manual alarm. Pull it during the Alarm step of RACE.

Fire extinguisher

For a small, contained fire only. Check the class label, then use PASS.

Fire blanket

Smothers a small fire, such as a pan or clothing fire, by cutting off oxygen.

Evacuation chair

Moves a person who cannot walk down the stairs during a vertical evacuation. Never use the elevator.

Assembly-point sign

Shows the route to the outdoor assembly point used in a full evacuation. Find yours this week.

Dr. Omar: Walk the corridor. Open each item: in a real fire you won't have time to look for them.

If you find a fire: RACE

Dr. Omar: People first, then the alarm, then close the doors. Only fight a small fire, with the right extinguisher: pull, aim, squeeze, sweep.

Put RACE in order

Smoke is coming from a consultation room. Put your actions in the right order.

  1. Rescue — move the patient out of the room
  2. Alarm — pull the call point and call the fire code
  3. Contain — close the door behind you
  4. Extinguish or evacuate — small fire: extinguisher; otherwise leave
Dr. Omar: Smoke from a consultation room. Put your four actions in order.

Using the extinguisher

A small bin fire. You have the right extinguisher. After you pull the pin, where do you aim?

Correct. The fuel is at the base: aim low, squeeze, sweep.

The flames are not the fuel. Aiming high wastes the extinguisher.

Smoke is not burning. Aim at the base of the fire.

Noor: One quick check on the extinguisher.

Five moments for clean hands

Noor: Two moments come before you touch, three come after. Watch where each one sits around the patient.

Which moment is it?

Drag each situation to its hand-hygiene moment.

You are about to take a patient's blood pressure
You are about to dress a wound
You have just emptied a urine bag
You have just helped a patient onto the couch
You have just adjusted the patient's bed rail and left
1 · Before touching a patient
2 · Before a clean / aseptic task
3 · After body-fluid exposure risk
4 · After touching a patient
5 · After touching patient surroundings
